extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, researchers, and general readers interested in media studies and political economy
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and applying Herman & Chomsky's propaganda model to evaluate how structural factors shape news selection and presentation; identifies filters and empirical indicators for diagnosing media bias. Useful for analyzing mainstream corporate media coverage and comparing allied vs. enemy-country reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: The size and profit-seeking imperative of dominant media corporations create a bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Herman and Chomsky argue that mainstream media outlets that are large corporations or part of conglomerates (e.g., Westinghouse or General Electric) will present information biased with respect to owners' interests. Conglomerates' extensive financial interests may be endangered by certain information, so news that most endangers corporate financial interests faces greatest bias and censorship. Historical context: earlier radical/worker-friendly papers were less constrained by corporate ownership; rising costs and corporate concentration reduced diversity. Implication for evaluation: examine ownership structures, cross-industry holdings, and potential conflicts of interest when assessing why particular topics are downplayed or emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding generated through advertising shapes news: the product is affluent/readers (the audience) sold to advertisers; news becomes 'filler' to attract customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most newspapers must attract advertising to cover production costs; competition for advertisers influences content. Stories that conflict with advertisers' 'buying mood' are marginalized or excluded. The model frames news as the means to deliver privileged readers to advertisers — thus assess who advertises in a publication, dependence on particular industries, and whether coverage patterns align with advertisers' interests. Historical examples: demise of 'people's newspapers' linked to inability to attract advertising revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: The mass media are drawn into a symbiotic relationship with powerful sources of information by economic necessity and reciprocity of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large media concentrate reporters at central news 'terminals' (e.g., White House, Pentagon, 10 Downing Street) because they cannot place reporters everywhere. Dependence on official pronouncements, business corporations, and trade organizations makes media reluctant to run articles that will harm those sources or risk denial of access. This creates a 'moral division of labor' where 'officials have and give the facts' and 'reporters merely get them', encouraging an uncritical attitude. For evaluation: analyze source networks, frequency of official sources vs. independent or grassroots sources, and patterns of access-denial or retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flak
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative responses to a media statement or program (letters, calls, petitions, lawsuits, speeches, bills, etc.) that function as a disciplining mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flak is concerted effort to manage public information; business organizations can form 'flak machines' (example: Global Climate Coalition attacking climate scientists' credibility). Unlike market-derived filters, flak is characterized by organized punitive or reputational responses. Evaluation should look for organized campaigns of complaint, legal or political pressures, PR industry activity, and how outlets change coverage in response to flak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-Communism and fear (enemy/fear ideology)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideological filter (originally 'anticommunism') that exploits public fear/hatred of perceived enemies to shape news selection and framing; later iterations include 'war on terror' and Islamophobia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturing Consent identified anti-communism as a central ideological filter during the Cold War; Chomsky and Herman note it has shifted toward 'fear' (e.g., 'war on terror'). Anti-ideologies serve to frighten the public and justify acceptance of authority, and can be used to marginalize critics. For evaluation: examine recurrent enemy/terror framing, demonization of certain countries or groups, and how fear-based frames justify policies or marginalize dissent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of 'enemy' countries (foreign-coverage bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biases in foreign reporting that emphasize violence/genocide and unfavorable events in 'enemy' countries while downplaying or ignoring similar or worse abuses in allied countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors cite examples: emphasis on Soviet–Afghan War vs. lack of scrutiny of Vietnam War legality; highlighting genocide in Kosovo while ignoring greater genocide during Indonesian occupation of East Timor; favorable coverage of fraudulent elections in allied countries while unfavorable coverage of legitimate elections in enemy countries (e.g., Nicaragua). Use paired comparisons controlling for other factors when evaluating whether coverage disparity reflects bias. Evaluate topic selection, intensity, and valence of foreign reporting across countries with different geopolitical relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of scandals and leaks (selective scandalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media differential treatment of scandals and leaks—some revelations receive extensive coverage while others of equal or greater significance are ignored or minimized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chomsky contrasts coverage of Watergate with COINTELPRO and notes differential public attention. Another example: substantial coverage of the Afghan War Diaries vs. little coverage of a study on severe health problems in Fallujah. For evaluation: compare prominence, depth, and persistence of coverage for different scandals; assess whether coverage correlates with the political power of those implicated and the potential threat to elite interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology bias (use of loaded terms as indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of terminology (e.g., whether media call waterboarding 'torture') can indicate bias in framing and differential treatment depending on perpetrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harvard study found major US papers used the term 'torture' for waterboarding much less when the US government committed it (2002–2008) than when other countries did. Evaluators can track the use of specific loaded terms across comparable incidents to identify asymmetries in labeling that reflect bias or deference to powerful actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source balance/proportion (quantitative source analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion of sources cited (e.g., pro-war vs. anti-war) is an empirical indicator of bias in coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness and Accuracy In Reporting found disproportionate focus on pro-war sources in lead-up to the Iraq War, with anti-war sources making up a small percentage. Assessment involves counting and categorizing sources, measuring diversity of viewpoints, and comparing proportionate representation to independent baselines (e.g., public opinion, expert consensus).
